result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.has_bridges()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if the graph contains any bridge edges. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L32115-L32198){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.has_bridges() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Has bridges](/assets/graphs/has-bridges.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: two triangles joined only by the edge between C and D, a bridge (shown in the accent color) whose removal splits the graph, so has_bridges() returns True. Right: the same graph plus an edge between B and F (shown in the accent color), which gives every edge a detour, so has_bridges() returns False." width="100%"} A bridge (cut edge) is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components. In an undirected graph, an edge is a bridge exactly when it does not lie on any cycle. Use this method when you only need a yes/no answer; `bridges()` returns the bridge edge IDs themselves. Typical uses: - testing whether a network is 2-edge-connected (no single link failure can split it) - quick robustness screening of many graphs before a more detailed analysis - checking whether added redundancy has removed every single point of failure For directed graphs, an edge `u -> v` is reported as a bridge when it lies on no directed cycle, i.e. there is no way to get from `v` back to `u` without it. Under this definition every edge of a directed acyclic graph is a bridge, while a directed cycle has none. Isolated nodes and empty graphs have no edges and therefore no bridges. The method does not modify the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if at least one bridge exists, `False` otherwise. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For undirected graphs this runs Tarjan's bridge-finding DFS in $O(V + E)$ and checks whether any bridge was found. For directed graphs each edge is tested separately for a return path, which costs $O(E(V + E))$ in the worst case. Complete graphs and cycles both return `False`; trees return `True`, since every edge of a tree is a bridge. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A cycle has no single point of failure, so it has no bridges: ::: {#3e8bf44c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(5) graph.has_bridges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` False ``` ::: ::: A path is the opposite extreme: every edge is a bridge, since there's only one way to get from one end to the other: ::: {#ee230954 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(5) graph.has_bridges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Attaching a new node to the cycle by a single edge introduces exactly one bridge. The check now returns `True`, and `bridges()` can then be used to find out which edge it is: ::: {#e543a0e5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(4) graph.add_node(label="pendant") graph.add_edge(1, graph.get_id_from_label("pendant")) # Bridge to the new node graph.has_bridges(), len(graph.bridges()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (True, 1) ``` ::: ::: On a directed graph, an edge stops being a bridge once some path leads back from its target to its source. A directed chain has bridges, but closing it into a cycle removes them all: ::: {#2fa2c068 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} chain = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_path_graph(4) ring = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_cycle_graph(4) chain.has_bridges(), ring.has_bridges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
